stops.name: Vienna, birth in the clockmaker's household
stops.campa: Émile Henri Jaques is born in Vienna to a Swiss couple from Sainte-Croix, three generations of Vaudois pastors behind them: his father Jules represents the watchmakers of the Jura in the Austrian capital; his mother Julie Jaunin, trained in a Pestalozzi school, is herself a fine musician and teacher. From her he takes his first piano lessons at six, and with them the Pestalozzian conviction, planted before he can name it, that a child learns truly only through the body and the senses, never through the page alone.

stops.name: Geneva, the Conservatoire de Musique
stops.campa: In 1875 the family leaves Vienna and settles in Geneva, the true country of the boy's blood. At twelve he enters the Conservatoire de Musique, where the ordinary curriculum of solfège and harmony sits on him like a coat cut for someone else: dutiful, correct, and strangely mute. He excels without being moved. Decades later he will say that these very years, in which technically able students could not feel what they played, planted the first suspicion that something essential to music was being taught to the ear and withheld from the whole body.

stops.name: Geneva, the Belles-Lettres and La Soubrette
stops.campa: At sixteen, while still at university, he joins the Belles-Lettres literary society, Geneva's forge of young writers and performers, acting and composing among students who will remain his circle for life. That year he writes and stages his first operetta, La Soubrette, and founds a student orchestra he names Musigena. Music, theatre and comic invention are already inseparable in him: the same fusion that will, thirty years hence, be renamed eurhythmics and installed as a discipline in its own right.

stops.name: Paris: the Comédie-Française, Delibes, Fauré
stops.campa: At nineteen he goes to Paris to complete his training on two fronts at once, as if music alone could not hold him: acting under the great players of the Comédie-Française, Talbot chief among them, and composition under Léo Delibes and the young Gabriel Fauré, with Marmontel at the piano. He writes a comic opera, Riquet à la Houppe, and lives the double life of actor and composer that will mark every later stage-work: the pageants, the operas, the civic Festspiele, where music, movement and speech are never quite separated.

stops.name: Algiers, assistant conductor at the Théâtre des Nouveautés
stops.campa: A post as second conductor under the composer Adler brings him to Algiers, and the colonial theatre's routine repertoire is not what he remembers of these months. Beyond the pit, in the streets and cafés of the city, he hears for the first time drumming and dance whose rhythmic patterns answer to no bar-line he has been taught: quintuple and septuple measures, phrases that breathe against the beat rather than inside it, the human body itself keeping a time no European stave can fix. He begins, unofficially, to notate what he hears.

stops.name: Algiers, the theatre fails; a new name is taken
stops.campa: The Théâtre des Nouveautés goes bankrupt and the young conductor tours for a season with the scattering company rather than return at once to Europe, unwilling yet to let go of the rhythms that have unsettled him. It is in these Algiers years, chroniclers agree, that he adds Dalcroze to his birth name of Jaques: to be told apart from another composer of the same surname, but also, the canon likes to read, to mark the man who came home changed by a drum he cannot yet notate in any Conservatoire's terms.

stops.name: Vienna: Bruckner, Fuchs, Graedener
stops.campa: From the Algerian drum he returns, by way of Paris, to the city of his birth, and studies organ, piano and composition with Anton Bruckner, Robert Fuchs and Karl Graedener. Vienna gives him counterpoint and orchestration at the highest German bench; it does not touch what Algiers opened. He carries the two educations side by side, unreconciled, for the next five years: the strict harmonic science of the Conservatory and the wordless certainty that the body itself is a rhythmic instrument no harmony treatise addresses.

stops.name: Paris, Mathis Lussy and the science of musical rhythm
stops.campa: Back in Paris he meets Mathis Lussy, the Swiss theorist who has spent a life writing on the mechanics of musical rhythm, accent and nuance. The encounter is decisive: Lussy gives him a vocabulary and a rigor for the intuition Algiers first planted, the sense that rhythm is a bodily and physiological fact before it is a notated one. Within three years, appointed to teach in Geneva, he will begin turning Lussy's analysis and his own Algerian memory into a classroom method no Conservatoire has yet imagined.

stops.name: Geneva, appointed Professor of Harmony
stops.campa: At twenty-seven he is named Professor of Harmony and solfège at the Conservatoire de Musique de Genève, the institution that once taught him so correctly and so incompletely. From the first term he watches his own old affliction repeat itself in his pupils: fingers fluent on the keyboard, ears trained to name every interval, and bodies that cannot walk a bar of triple time without stumbling. He begins, quietly, to experiment: testing exercises whose subject is not the ear alone but the whole standing, breathing, weight-bearing person.

stops.name: Geneva: the desks removed, the jersey and bare feet
stops.campa: The experiments harden into a doctrine. He clears the desks from his classroom and makes the students stand and step the beat while they sing; he asks for loose jersey and bare feet in place of corset and heeled shoe, arguing that the body cannot answer music truthfully in clothes built to restrain it. Method piled on method, tested and discarded and tested again: he will say of these Geneva years only that he built the whole edifice by trying, over and over, to find the particular cause of each pupil's particular deafness of limb.
stops.quote: It is by trying to discover the individual cause of each musical defect, and to find a means of correcting it, that I have gradually built up my method of eurhythmics. This method is entirely based upon experiments many times repeated.
stops.quote_source: Jaques-Dalcroze, 'Rhythm as a Factor in Education', in Rhythm, Music and Education (trans. Ingham, 1921)

stops.name: Geneva, Poème alpestre at the National Exhibition
stops.campa: The Swiss National Exhibition opens on the Plaine de Plainpalais, and Jaques-Dalcroze is entrusted with the Poème alpestre, the official Festspiel of the fair: massed choirs, an orchestra, and a libretto of mountains and cowherds staged before thousands. It is his first great civic pageant, the form he will return to at every turning of his life, and already it fuses what the Conservatoire keeps separate: music, poetry, and the moving crowd as a single instrument of national feeling, rehearsed like a rhythmic-gymnastics class scaled to a whole canton.

stops.name: Geneva, marriage to Nina Faliero
stops.campa: On the day after Christmas he marries the Italian soprano Maria-Anna Starace, who sings under the stage name Nina Faliero and who will take leading roles in several of his own operas in the years ahead. The household she keeps becomes the quiet counterweight to the classroom battles at the Conservatoire: a working artist's marriage, music at both ends of the table, in the city that will, through every later upheaval, remain the fixed point he returns to.
